### Locked Out of China’s AI Boom, Graduates Turn to Bootcamps

When Wu Jianhua graduated from college in June 2024, China’s AI industry seemed to be hiring everyone except her. Desperate for a way in, she turned to AI tutorials on social media.

“But the videos were mostly aimed at professionals and used very complex language,” the 24-year-old told Sixth Tone.

So when a friend who had completed the program and landed a job told her about a three-month AI training bootcamp in Beijing, Wu decided to give it a shot. By the end of March, she had learned Python, the programming language, and landed a job as an AI Junior Trainer, one of a growing number of entry-level roles supporting China’s AI boom.

“Unlike the videos I found online, the courses broke concepts down with examples,” Wu said.

Wu is one of a growing number of Chinese graduates turning to short-term training programs as competition for jobs intensifies. With the number of new graduates rising from 7.65 million in 2016 to 12.7 million this year, many are finding that employers increasingly value practical skills over academic credentials alone.

To close that gap, local governments have rolled out short-term training programs tied to fast-growing occupations. The courses range from AI-related work and drone piloting to health care and elder care.

Whether a few months of training can translate into a lasting career remains a subject of debate. For now, demand for such programs appears to be growing.

Bootcamp

The job Wu landed was less glamorous than the title might suggest. Rather than designing AI models, junior AI trainers spend much of their time cleaning, organizing, and analyzing data to help improve AI products.

To prepare students for that work, the bootcamp at the Beijing AI Future Vocational Education School began with Python, widely used to process and analyze large datasets. Trainees were also introduced to workplace AI tools commonly encountered on the job.

Unlike the tutorials she had found online, the bootcamp followed a structured curriculum. Wu reinforced lessons through practical exercises and could turn to instructors and teaching assistants on messaging app WeChat whenever she got stuck.

“The instructors would go over the questions people kept running into and explain the difficult parts again,” Wu said. “There were also regular quizzes, so you always knew whether you were keeping up.”

Since March, more than 1,500 people have completed training through the Beijing school, many of them unemployed and looking to improve their job prospects through new skills, according to Zhao Xuesong, a partner and board member of the institution.

One of the biggest challenges, Zhao said, is correcting misconceptions about the field. Many trainees assume AI training means learning to program or build AI systems, when much of the work involves translating business needs into data, feeding that data into models, fine-tuning and deploying the solutions, and driving continuous iteration to enhance AI usability.

“We need to explain clearly that AI training is not the same as programming or coding,” she said.

The program combines self-paced online coursework with hands-on training led by university instructors and industry professionals. Tuition ranges from 1,200 yuan to 2,400 yuan ($170 to $335), depending on the course level.

Graduates who find work as junior AI trainers through the program typically start at around 5,000 yuan a month, according to Zhao. Roughly 85% of trainees pass the certification exam on their first attempt, while those who fail can retake both the course and exam free of charge.

After completing the program in March, Wu was introduced to potential employers through the school and soon began interviewing for positions. Zhao said the institution maintains long-term partnerships with domestic tech companies including Alibaba, ByteDance, Tencent, and Baidu.

“Without the institution, I might not know which companies are hiring for this role. I would be in a relatively closed information loop,” Wu said.

She now works largely remotely and, aside from a weekly team meeting, enjoys a flexible schedule.

Plan B

When Li Jiaxin signed up for an AI training program last August, she was looking for any job that offered some semblance of stability: a steady salary, weekends off, social insurance, and housing fund benefits.

Fresh out of college, Li had spent months applying for video-editing jobs without success. As classmates found work or moved on to graduate school, she grew increasingly anxious. “I just wanted to get ashore,” she said.

Despite having no prior experience in artificial intelligence, Li landed a job as a junior AI trainer after completing the training. The role involves creating videos, learning new AI tools, and working on-site from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Not everyone is convinced that such programs are a long-term solution. Short-term training courses risk narrowing education into a quick pipeline for producing job-ready workers, said Ma Jiuyuan, a career advisor at Shanghai’s Fudan University.

Without unified certification standards or reliable public data on employment outcomes and salaries, graduates may struggle to distinguish between serious training providers and expensive anxiety-driven bootcamps. Ma said she has seen students enroll in costly AI-generated content courses hoping to gain an edge, only to discover that the curriculum covered little more than basic generative AI tools.

At the same time, employers increasingly favor candidates with practical experience, Ma said. “A graduate with only textbook knowledge may be eliminated at the résumé screening stage.” For that reason, she argued, short-term training can help bridge the “last mile” between campus and the workplace.

Ma also acknowledged the policy’s role in easing structural mismatches in the labor market, particularly for vocational students, applied undergraduates, and graduates seeking to switch careers. She nevertheless called for stronger oversight, including greater transparency around employment outcomes and salaries.

Yu Zhuanzong, an associate professor at Fudan University and career planner, expects demand for such programs to continue to grow. As industries evolve faster than university curricula, graduates increasingly need short, practical courses to update their skills after leaving campus, he said.

Li can already see the demand among her peers. Many of her former classmates remain in traditional industries, and she said she would recommend the program to those looking for a different path.

“It’s at least a fallback,” she said. “And if you do well, the instructors may recommend you for better jobs.”

Her own ambitions have expanded as well. “As I go deeper into the industry, my goals have become clearer,” she said.

“Beyond a stable job and a good work environment, I want to build my professional skills so that I qualify for more roles and eventually earn a higher salary.”

Editor: Apurva.

### Did AI Find Murakami’s Voice? Student’s $2 Experiment Divides China’s Literati

Chinese readers of Haruki Murakami used to wait over a year for a faithful Mandarin translation of his latest book after its official release in Japanese. Not this time.

An unlicensed, high-fidelity digital version of the author’s new novel, “The Tale of KAHO,” was available to download in Chinese just hours after it went on sale in Tokyo on July 3.

There were no lengthy negotiations over rights, no translators straining to make a deadline, no pondering on how to capture Murakami’s distinct voice. Instead, it was accomplished in a relative flash for less than $2 using an AI-based tool developed by a 21-year-old university student.

“The Tale of KAHO,” a novel about a picture book illustrator who slips between dream and reality, was the first real test for Wenyi, a coding project that instructs large-language-model artificial intelligence on literary translation. Its designer, who asked to be identified by the pseudonym Ping Ming for privacy reasons, says he wanted to know whether AI could handle not only simple text but also glossary management, polishing, and rounds of spontaneous self-reviews.

What he discovered could fundamentally alter how novels are translated.

Wenyi’s unlicensed translation of the novel quickly began circulating on Chinese social media and the resale platform Xianyu, as well as the free online archive Z-Library.

Anecdotal evidence suggests readers are impressed. On China’s interest-oriented networking platform Douban, the most-liked review of the novel reads, “If this is purely AI translation, the quality is astonishing! … If AI can already do this much, what’s the point of having human translators?”

Readers might be happy, but publishing industry insiders feel AI still has a long way to go before it can replace humans — while legal experts warn that copyright holders could lose out either way.

Staying faithful

Nanshan Youlu, a part-time Japanese-to-Chinese translator who asked to use his online alias, worked with a friend on a manual translation of “The Tale of KAHO,” which they also began sharing bit by bit on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, on July 3.

Their first post received more than 2,000 likes, with many users expressing gratitude and complimenting the quality of their translation. Yet shortly after completing the final chapter, the duo wiped their version from the internet, citing that Wenyi’s translation was just too good — virtually 100% faithful to the original Japanese text.

“When human translators work on a novel, they will read the whole book first, and therefore will build their own interpretation and create their own ‘context.’ It’s basically impossible for them to achieve 100% wording fidelity,” Nanshan Youlu, a 30-something working at a tech company in Beijing, tells Sixth Tone. “They don’t translate mechanically — every sentence they translate serves the context they build.”

Wenyi works differently. Ping explains that his program started by dividing the book into chunks of fewer than 2,000 words, which it then sent one by one to the Chinese AI model DeepSeek for translation. To maintain continuity, each chunk overlapped by six paragraphs. “If you feed AI tens of thousands of words all at once, there’s a risk of AI hallucination, which can result in lots of mistakes,” he says.

The program also asked AI to extract important terms and proper nouns from the material so it can continuously update a glossary of keywords to ensure consistency. Once finished, the system reviews the entire book — again, chunk by chunk — to check for problems.

Not a single human had read the Chinese translation before Ping uploaded it to Z-Library just four hours after the official version of the novel was released in Japan. The project had cost him just 13 yuan ($1.90) in DeepSeek tokens.

However, once online, he soon began noticing mistakes. Some nouns, such as the various nicknames for the protagonist Kaho, hadn’t been extracted for the glossary and were inconsistent, while some wording was unnatural, more machine-like.

He decided to translate it again, this time refining his code to instruct the AI to be more meticulous about names, and requesting a complete polish of the text. This second version was better, he says, although it took longer.

Ping, a literature major at Nanjing Normal University in the eastern Jiangsu province, taught himself to code using the Python programming language two years ago. To train Wenyi, he used English-language literature including works by the 19th-century American writer Edgar Allan Poe and Scottish novelist Ian McEwan.

“When I was a child, I always found hackers in the movies so cool, and I wanted to have those skills,” Ping tells Sixth Tone, adding that in more recent years he has been attracted by the rapid developments in AI technology.

The idea for Wenyi partially stemmed from his passion for literature. As a fan of Murakami, Ping always wanted to read the author’s books as soon as they were released, but he can’t read Japanese. He recalls attempting to digest an unlicensed Mandarin version of Murakami’s novel “The City and Its Uncertain Walls” produced using the free DeepL online translation tool in 2023, “but it was unacceptably bad — the grammar, pronouns, proper nouns, all were a mess.” He had to wait another year for the official Chinese version, translated by the prominent literary scholar Shi Xiaowei.

Machine translation has been around a while, but conventional tools have never been considered good enough for literary works.

“Someone needs to step forward and explore how good AI translation can be,” says Ping. “If it were not me, it would be someone else. … The original AI models set the lower limit (of translation), while Wenyi sets the upper limit.”

However, not everyone is impressed. Lin Shaohua, who translated Murakami’s earlier works, including the best-sellers “Kafka on the Shore” and “Norwegian Wood,” told China Newsweek that while Wenyi’s translation was technically fluent, it had failed to capture the author’s true voice.

“AI translation has achieved ‘grammatically coherent and reads smoothly’ — but that’s all,” he’s quoted as saying. “AI is still not quite capable of conveying subtle nuances of language and stylistic nuances. … The story itself is not literature. Only its particular tone makes it literature. Literature is the art of language.”

However, over the years, Lin has faced criticism from readers over alleged mistakes in his translations that might have changed what the original author intended to convey.

Nanshan Youlu believes this is hard to avoid and sees translation as a continuation of the creative process. While some translators aim to follow an author’s style to the letter, for him, the core of the job is to convey the feelings in a text, rather than reproduce the exact wording. Sometimes, after working for hours on a draft, he will review it and find areas that aren’t exactly faithful to the source novel — though revising them might disrupt the structure and context that he’s already built.

“If you read the AI translation closely, you’ll find it’s quite fragmented when it comes to context,” he says. “There’s a certain disharmony to it, a sense that the whole thing was pieced together.”

However, for Ping, fidelity to the original is essential. “If a translation doesn’t match, I’d simply call it a mistake — that’s non-negotiable,” he says. “No matter how good your education and cultural literacy, or how beautiful and fluent your translations are, if you’re not faithful to the original, there’s nothing to talk about.”

There be pirates

Of course, without a licensing agreement, both Ping Ming and Nanshan Youlu risk accusations of copyright infringement for releasing their translations online, regardless of whether they profited financially.

Under China’s Copyright Law, using published works for personal study, research, or appreciation is considered fair use. However, this doesn’t apply if the use is seen as harmful to the copyright holder’s rights and interests — for example, negatively affecting sales of Murakami’s books in China.

“The nonprofit nature of their conduct does not constitute grounds for exemption from liability,” Zhang Jie, an attorney from Shanghai-based law firm Zhihe Partners with experience handling intellectual property (IP) disputes, tells Sixth Tone. “The law’s control over acts such as reproduction, adaptation, translation, and dissemination via information networks naturally extends to the use of AI. Whether infringement has occurred has little to do with whether a work was created by a human or with AI assistance.”

She adds that China legally protects the IP rights of overseas authors under the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works and other international treaties.

While this initial breakthrough in AI literary translation may have skirted the law, it does demonstrate the technology’s potential legitimate use by publishing houses. However, industry insiders suggest the overwhelming preference is still for human translators, especially when handling more complex projects.

Liu Chengxu, an editor at Guangdong People’s Publishing House, says, “If the original book is straightforward to understand, I’d choose AI translation. Frankly speaking, in those cases, there isn’t much difference between the work of a seasoned human translator and that of an AI translator. But if the original is more complex, like if it’s hard sci-fi or a thought experiment, I would choose a human translator.”

Compared with the lightning speed of DeepSeek, a professional translator will need about six months to complete a 350-page book like “The Tale of KAHO.” Then come editorial reviews, proofreading, publication, and distribution, with the book finally hitting shelves after about a year. Meanwhile, translators earn 100 to 120 yuan per 1,000 characters — not a high rate, but still far more than the current cost of AI.

Despite the obvious benefits, Puzhao, an editor at the Shanghai Translation Publishing House who goes by a pen name, feels that using AI to translate fiction still isn’t a viable option. “I prefer collaborating with humans,” he says. “When it comes to literary books, we need humans to translate them in their own words.”

He cites Emily Wilson’s acclaimed 2017 version of Homer’s epic “The Odyssey” as an example that a new translation of a classical or even modern text has the power to spark widespread discussion. This, he says, demonstrates that translation is not merely a mechanical transfer of words but a way to use contemporary language to introduce stories to new audiences.

On an ethical level, Puzhao concedes that he dislikes AI translation because it “deprives humans of job opportunities,” adding that people “put so much time and effort into creating original content, only for some tech monopoly to feed it into AI training. All we can do is make some small acts of resistance. My position is non-cooperation.”

In the summer of 2023, China introduced the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services, requiring tech companies to carry out training activities only with data from lawful sources and to guard against IP infringement.

Whether Ping’s experiment will fundamentally change the future of literary translation is yet to be seen — but it’s certainly got people reading into the consequences.

Editor: Hao Qibao.
